steps.action:
The lighthouse at Breaker’s Point had been lit every night for seventy-two years, and for fifty-three of those, Elias Kerr had climbed its iron steps.

The tower rose from the black teeth of rock like a bone pointing at heaven. In winter storms, waves shattered against its base and sprayed its narrow windows with brine. In summer, gulls nested on its ledges and screamed at the dawn. The paint on its sea-facing side had been scoured to a dull gray by wind and salt. Only the landward side still remembered that it had once been white.

The town on the cliff above called it “the Old Eye.” That was what people said in the pub, in the empty hour after the last ferry left and the quiet grew heavy: “The Old Eye’s watching,” or, on kinder days, “Elias will see them through.” Most of them had never been inside the tower. They spoke of it the way they spoke of weather and of the dead—inevitable, unfathomable, taken for granted.

Elias did not think of it as an eye. To him, the lens room at the top was a heart: a glass heart, beating with rotations and flares instead of muscle and blood. And he was less its keeper than its attendant, a thin old man in a navy watch coat, moving through its chambers with oil can and rag and the slow, unhurried care of someone who has learned that breaking things is easy and mending things is work.

Every evening began the same.

When the sun had dipped until only a smear of brass clung to the horizon, Elias would push himself up from the kitchen chair, set his cup of tea beside the sink, and test his knees with one small shift of weight. They complained faintly, but not enough to stop him. He hung the battered brass keyring from his belt, shrugged into his coat, and checked—by habit, not necessity—that his logbook and pencil were where they always were on the shelf by the door.

He stepped out into the narrow yard between the cottage and the tower. The wind insisted on being noticed, tugging at his coat, bringing him the familiar smells: cold iron, distant fish guts from the harbor, damp earth from the path down from town. The last colors drained from the sea as he crossed to the tower door.

The lock turned with a clack and a squeal. The door breathed out stale dampness. Elias flicked on the light in the entrance chamber—a bare bulb under a wire cage—and the spiral of stairs rose up and up, disappearing into shadow where the light could not reach.

He began to climb.

Forty-nine steps to the storeroom landing, where spare wicks and fuel cans once sat. The big oil tanks had been long since removed; the light had gone electric in the seventies and automated in the nineties. Still, Elias counted the steps. It was part of the rhythm that held him together.

Sixty-three steps to the observation landing. He paused there each night, as he always did, to look out through the small, round window. The town’s yellow lights clung to the cliff’s edge like a necklace on a bony throat. Beyond, the land fell away into dark. The forums up in the city had once argued whether Breaker’s Point lighthouse was still needed, now that new navigation systems and GPS satellites watched the ocean from orbit. No screen had yet learned how to look the way this tower did: with stubbornness, with a single-minded devotion to a very small patch of sea.

They had cut staff, of course. Once there had been three keepers. Then two. Now there was Elias, and the automation that had come in a crate. The papers he had signed had been kind, on the whole. They called him “senior attendant” instead of “the last one.”

He climbed again.

At the top, he unlocked the hatch to the lantern room. The familiar smell met him: machine oil, old glass, faint baked dust from the machinery. The great Fresnel lens loomed around him—a crystal cathedral of rings and prisms tall enough to swallow him whole. Outside, the world was wind and gray sea and night.

He ran his hand, gently, along the metal rail of the service gallery, feeling for any roughness or grime. His fingers had grown uncertain over the years; he distrusted them now and relied on routine more than touch. Still, they found a bit of salt crust where the last storm had blown spray through a bad seal. He took a rag from his pocket and rubbed it away, listening to the faint, proportioned scrape.

The light was already lit. It always was, these days. A sensor in a box on the outside of the lantern tower measured the fall of the day and sent a pulse by copper wire to the lamp. If the sensor failed, a timer would wake the backup. If the timer failed, a second lamp would hum to life. Somewhere in the workshop of a harbor authority engineer, there was a diagram of all the ways Breaker’s Point Light could fail, and red lines circling them, and notes in careful handwriting: test monthly; inspect annually.

If everything failed, there was still Elias.

He checked the lamp’s housing, the cables, the tiny indicator lights. Then he turned to the panel where a row of toggles waited like the fingers of a sleeping hand. He flipped the one that switched off the automation and surrendered control to manual.

The great lens turned.

The light, once in a steady, dumb glow, now began its slow, even rotation: four seconds of shining, twelve of darkness, four of shining again. A signature encoded in the roll of light, a pulse that every ship’s chart carried in a column beside its name: Breaker’s Point Light—Fl 4s, eclipsed 12s, range 23 nmi.

No ship in sight at the moment, just the dark.

Elias eased into the narrow wooden chair that had belonged to his predecessor, pulled a folded blanket over his knees, and reached for the logbook. The ritual words came as they always did.

“1830 hours. Lamp tested, rotation engaged. Visibility eight miles. Wind from the northwest. Sea state moderate. Automation override: manual watch.”

He paused, pencil hovering, then added, almost as an afterthought: “Meteor shower expected.”

This last note was not required. There was no box for it on the form. It would puzzle the clerk at the harbor office who later transcribed these lines into an unseen database. But Elias wrote it anyway.

Because tonight was his last official watch.

They had told him two months ago, in the office above the ferry dock, where the wallpaper was still angrily orange from the seventies. The man who told him—the same one who had quietly arranged for his pension paperwork and his medical forms, all those decades ago—was older now, with white hair and a belly grown sleepy over his belt.

“It’s time, Eli,” the harbormaster had said. “You’ve done your share and more. We’ve upgraded all the systems. We’ll still have someone out to check the place twice a week. But there’ll be no more night watch here.”

Elias had looked out through the window at the line where sea met sky. He had imagined it unguarded, a single blank stretch of dark. His chest tightened, as though someone had put a hand around the bone bars of his ribs and squeezed.

“It isn’t as if you’ve had much to do for a while,” the harbormaster had added, kindly enough. “Any fool can see the light ten miles off. The computers don’t sleep. Besides, the new buoys all talk to the ships now. She doesn’t need you like she used to.”

“She?” Elias had said, still watching the horizon. “Who says she doesn’t?”

He had not argued, in the end. He had done his nodding, his signing. There was a dignity in knowing when the tide had turned and not standing knee-deep in it, shouting. But that night, and the next, and every night until this one, he had walked up to the lighthouse with a new awareness in his steps, as if each footfall were a word in a sentence nearing its period.

Now, in the lantern room, the meteor shower’s first faint streaks scratched white scars over the eastern sky. He had heard about it on the radio—that it would peak just after midnight, that there would be a good view from the coast if the clouds stayed away. The announcer’s voice had been too bright, promising wishes. As if anyone over seventy believed in wishes.

He believed in the turning of things: the lens, the earth, the endless circulation of salt water and wind and ships outlines passing in the night.

He closed the logbook and leaned back. The room rocked slowly around him as the lens moved, throwing its revolving beam out over the water. In the intervals of darkness, the faint meteor streaks were easier to see. In the bursts of light, they vanished.

One of his earliest memories of the lighthouse had been of his mother carrying him up the steps. He had been four, perhaps five. His father had still been the keeper then, a broad-shouldered man with a black beard salted white near the chin. The old oil lamp had rumbled inside its casing, a dragon in iron skin. Glass prisms, taller than his mother, had towered above him.

“That’s it,” his father had said, when they reached the top. “Mind your hands; everything in here bites.” His voice had been gentle, but the words had stuck. The room had seemed alive, humming and ticking. His father had moved through it with purpose, a man amid an organ of glass.

“You tell him what it does,” his mother had said, nudging him.

“This?” His father had raised an eyebrow, then had crouched so his face was level with Elias’. “This is a promise,” he said. “This says ‘Here I am’ to anyone out there who’s lost. That’s what a lighthouse is: a promise someone made a long time ago that we still keep, every night.”

It was only years later, standing drenched and shaking by the radio, that Elias had realized promises could be one-way things.

The storm that took his father rose so quickly the barometer could barely keep up. A trawler had gone quiet on the wireless after a broken, half-heard call. His father had gone out with the lifeboat crew while Elias, eighteen then and home on leave from his first job as an apprentice mechanic inland, had argued.

“It’s madness,” he had said. “You can’t even see the harbor mouth from here. The waves—”

“They know the risk,” his father had said simply as he shrugged into his heavy coat. “We know it. The sea doesn’t care if we go or stay, but if we stay, and they drown, and we did nothing—”

He had not finished the sentence. He had not needed to. Elias had understood that for his father there had never really been a choice.

The trawler was found three days later, its hull torn open, its nameplate splintered but just readable. Of the lifeboat, nothing. People spoke in that special, hushed tone reserved for those lost at sea—as if speaking too loud might call the water’s attention to them and invite it to claim more.

After the funeral without a body, after his mother’s brief, silent rage against the sea and the harbor and God, the letters had come. One from the harbor authority, asking if the family wished to leave the cottage and take up residence closer to town. Another, weeks later, asking if Elias might be interested in applying for a junior position at the lighthouse.

He had not wanted to. He had wanted to leave, to go inland, to work on engines that rolled on firm roads instead of floating on the backs of waves. But his mother’s grief pinned her to the coast, and there was the small matter of money that had always been small and suddenly seemed minuscule. And the tower up on Breaker’s Point did not feel like the thing that had taken his father from him. It felt like the only thing that understood.

So he had climbed the steps again, and again, and again, across five decades, until the way his knees blew out smoke on cold mornings felt as familiar to him as the lighthouse’s slow, sweeping blink.

The meteor shower thickened. The stars seemed to fray at the edges as pieces of them fell, burning. Out there, beyond the black horizon, ships moved with their own lights: white for the bow, green and red for port and starboard, amber glows from deck lamps, all plotted and charted and watched by machines far more patient than any man.

A faint buzz sounded from the radio on the shelf.

He leaned forward, flicked it on, and turned the knob until the static thinned.

“…Breaker’s Point, this is Coastwatch Relay. Routine check. Over.”

Elias pressed the transmit key. “Breaker’s Point receiving. Light operational. Manual watch in progress. Visibility good. Over.”

“Copy that, Breaker’s. Enjoy the show up there. Last one under your care, eh?” The voice on the other end was young, with an accent from two counties away. They rotated the Coastwatch operators through posts so none of them grew complacent, a bureaucrat’s shield against routine.

Elias hesitated. “That’s what they tell me,” he said. “Over.”

“Well, we appreciate you. My dad says your light saved his ferry more than once when the fog played tricks on him. Clear skies, Breaker’s. Relay out.”

The line clicked. The room filled again with the quiet, omnipresent sound of machinery. Elias turned the knob to off. He sat back. “We appreciate you,” the young man had said, as if it were a thing you could put in an envelope and post.

He did not know the voice’s name. He knew the sea, though, and the exact color it turned an hour before a storm, and the way light bounced off different hull paints, and how many beats his heart took to carry him from the cottage door to the base of the tower steps.

He had measured his life in such intervals.

At half past eleven, he made tea on the small gas ring in the service nook just below the lantern room. He had learned to pour without spilling in rough weather by bracing his elbow against the wall, letting the swaying of the tower guide his wrist. Tonight the sea was almost calm. The cup trembled only from his fingers.

He brought the tea back up to the glass room, cradling it in both hands, and lowered himself into the chair again. The meteor shower was at its height now. Lines of white scratched and vanished. The beam swept, wiped them from sight, then revealed new ones where none had been the moment before. The sky became an enormous, silent etch-a-sketch.

Elias remembered, unexpectedly vividly, his daughter as a child pressing her nose against this very glass, her breath fogging it in small, determined patches. “Why do they fall?” she had asked, watching another streak dissolve.

“Because they have to,” he had said then, wanting an answer quickly. He had not been as patient as he intended, sometimes, when his mind was split between the demands of the tower and the sudden, ferocious presence of another fragile life. “Gravity pulls. Same as it keeps us here.”

“How do they know where to go?” she persisted.

“Well, that’s someone else’s job,” he had said, and had regretted the snap in his tone for hours after she had gone to sleep. It had seemed, in that moment, unfair that the sky could pour out so much beauty without needing anyone to tend it, to polish and wind and check readings.

She had left at nineteen, carrying a suitcase lighter than his had been at that age but somehow feeling heavier. She had gone inland, as he had once imagined he might, to a city of glass offices and windows that did not leak in a storm. They spoke at holidays. They wrote, infrequently. Each time, she asked if he had thought about leaving yet. Each time, he changed the subject gently, the way one might stroke a cat that had just unsheathed its claws.

Who would he be, away from this narrow world? An old man in a rented room with photos of ships he no longer saw?

He sipped his tea. The heat made the inside of his chest bloom.

At a quarter to midnight, a shadow moved in the corner of his vision. He turned his head. Far to the east, where the shipping lane bent in its long arc, a small cluster of lights had appeared. White, red, green: the textbook colors of a vessel moving steadily along its plot.

Elias stood. He put the tea down. Without thinking, he reached for the binoculars that hung from a hook exactly where they had hung since before he was born. He brought them to his eyes.

The ship was small, maybe forty meters. Cargo, he thought, noting the boxiness of the stern, the low line of the bow. Older model. It rode low in the water, burdened. Its lights wavered a little more than they should have, swooning with the waves rather than cutting through them. He frowned.

He adjusted the focus. Numbers came into clarity on the bow: CARRIETTA. A flag fluttered from the mast—a country he did not recognize at once, horizontal stripes in a sequence he had not had reason to memorize. No AIS information came through the small repeater screen bolted to the wall. That was odd. Modern vessels broadcast their identification like birdsong.

The meteor shower scribbled silently behind the ship. The beam from the lighthouse swept over it, bathing the hull in a wash of white. For the brief interval when the light and the ship aligned, its paint looked scabbed, rusty. Salt had eaten more of it than any inspectors would like.

He lowered the glass. The old part of his mind, the pre-automation, oil-lamp-trained part, murmured. He took a breath and listened.

The ship’s course was fine as far as the lane went—but the night’s currents were tricksy around Breaker’s Point, playing games with captains who trusted their charts more than their eyes. He had seen ships creeper closer in heavy fog, watched their ghost-glimmer appear where no sane navigator would put them.

The new systems on his panel flashed no alarms. The chart plotter showed a ribbon of intended path far enough from the rocks. The harbor authority’s radio channel was quiet.

He watched the CARRIETTA for three more sweeps of the beam.

On the fourth, he saw the angle of its bow had shifted, subtle but unmistakable, toward the land.

He did not think. He reached for the radio, flicked it on, and set his old finger on the transmit button.

“Unidentified cargo vessel bearing east by southeast, this is Breaker’s Point Lighthouse. You are altering course shoreward. State your condition. Over.”

Silence hissed back at him. The meteor shower fell. The ship’s lights jolted again, like a drunk’s attempt to stand upright.

He tried again, adding the old, nearly forgotten words: “Vessel CARRIETTA, this is Breaker’s Point. You are heading toward shoal water. Correct to seaward. Repeat: alter course to seaward. Over.”
